extracted.intended_audience: state environmental agencies, regulated power plant owners/operators, industry stakeholders, technical experts, and commenters on EPA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_short: EGU emission guidelines for combustion turbines
extracted.subtask_description: Federal EPA preamble and technical support describing standards of performance, cost and operational assumptions, and monitoring/reporting expectations for electric generating units (especially combined cycle/combustion turbines) under greenhouse gas emission guidelines. Includes formulas, amortization and capacity-factor assumptions, and references to technical/ISO standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER is CCS with 90 percent capture
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA uses the two phrases (i) BSER is CCS with 90 percent capture and (ii) CCS with 90 percent capture is achievable, or similar phrases, interchangeably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes CCS achieving ~90% capture as the best system of emission reduction (BSER) for the applicable subcategory; statements in the rule and analyses should treat the two phrasings as equivalent when describing the standard of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment, monitoring, mass-balance, and documentation requirements (subpart RR and VV / CSA/ANSI ISO 27916:2019)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both subpart RR and subpart VV (CSA/ANSI ISO 27916:2019) require an assessment and monitoring of potential leakage pathways; quantification of inputs, losses, and storage through a mass balance approach; and documentation of steps and approaches used to establish these quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing monitoring/reporting for CO2 storage/use (including CO2-EOR), ensure: (1) potential leakage pathways are assessed and monitored; (2) inputs, losses, and stored CO2 are quantified using a mass-balance methodology; and (3) the methods and steps used to derive those quantities are fully documented. Note primary differences between subparts relate to the terms used in mass-balance equations, definitions of leakage, and rules for when facilities may discontinue reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emission-rate calculation for a new small natural gas-fired base load EGU
rubrics_metrics.description: As proposed, a new small natural gas-fired base load EGU would determine the facility emissions rate by taking the difference in the base load rating and 250 MMBtu/h, multiplying that number by 0.0743 lb CO2/(MW * MMBtu), and subtracting that number from 900 lb CO2/MWh-gross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: for a natural gas-fired base load combustion turbine with a base load rating of 1,000 MMBtu/h, the calculation is 900 lb CO2/MWh-gross minus (1,000 - 250 = 750 MMBtu/h * 0.0743 lb CO2/(MW*MMBtu)) = 844 lb CO2/MWh-gross. Use this formulaic approach to compute facility-specific emission-rate standards for similarly categorized units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat-input-based fuel-adjustment methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: The heat input-based emission rates of natural gas and distillate oil are 117 and 163 lb CO2/MMBtu, respectively. The ratio of the heat input-based emission rates (1.39) is multiplied by the natural gas-fired standard of performance (770 lb CO2/MWh) to get the applicable emissions rate (1,070 lb CO2/MWh).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To adjust an emissions-rate standard for alternate fossil fuels, multiply the applicable heat-input-based emission-rate ratio by the baseline fuel's standard. Apply the specific lb CO2/MMBtu values cited when performing these fuel-conversion calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity-factor assumptions for cost and compliance calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: The compliance costs assume the same capacity factors in the base and policy case, that is, without CCS and with CCS. The EPA used a constant 65 percent capacity factor in some calculations but also considers using a higher capacity factor for the first 12 years and a lower one thereafter to reflect actual operating conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating compliance costs, explicitly state whether capacity factors are held constant between base/policy cases or varied over time. Recognize that using a higher capacity factor during the initial 12-year period (e.g., when 45Q tax benefits are available) will produce lower compliance costs than assuming identical capacity factors across cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amortization periods for CCS and CO2 transport/storage & monitoring (TS&M) costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The CCS and CO2 TS&M costs are amortized over the period the equipment is operated—30 years or 12 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the amortization period based on expected equipment operation and policy/tax-credit windows. For existing coal-fired units EPA calculated CCS costs using a 12-year amortization period aligned with the 45Q tax credit availability (assuming equipment is amortized over the 12-year credit period and no operation is assumed after that period for cost recovery). For new or long-lived installations, a 30-year amortization may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic assumptions used in CCS cost calculations (service life, interest rate, fuel price, capacity factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: For consistency with the proposal's assumption capacity factor, these calculations use a service life of 30 years, an interest rate of 7.0 percent, a natural gas price of $3.61/MMBtu, and a capacity factor of 65 percent. These costs do not include CO2 transport, storage, or monitoring costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reproducing or comparing EPA cost estimates, use the stated baseline economic assumptions (30-year service life, 7.0% interest, $3.61/MMBtu gas, 65% capacity factor) and note that transport, storage, and monitoring costs are excluded unless otherwise specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for increased auxiliary load when converting capture percentage to percent reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The 89 percent reduction from CCS accounts for the increased auxiliary load of a 90 percent post combustion amine-based capture system. Due to rounding, the proposed numeric standards of performance do not necessarily match the standards that would be determined by applying the percent reduction to the phase-1 standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When converting a capture-efficiency assumption (e.g., 90% capture) into a percent reduction of facility emissions, account for the capture system's auxiliary energy requirements, which reduce net output and alter lb/MWh rates. Expect minor inconsistencies due to rounding when reporting final numeric standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of NETL H-Class and F-Class model plants and turbine-size normalization
rubrics_metrics.description: As explained in the TSD, the 6,100 MMBtu/h H-Class combustion turbine is the median size of recently constructed combined cycle facilities and the 4,600 MMBtu/h F-Class combustion turbine approximates the size of a number of recently constructed combined cycle facilities as well. CCS costs for smaller sources are higher but are not prohibitive. To estimate an achievable emissions rate for an efficient combined cycle EGU at 250 MMBtu/h the EPA assumed a linear relationship for combined cycle efficiency with turbine engines with base load ratings of less than 2,000 MMBtu/h.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use NETL model plant sizes (H-class and F-class) as benchmarking points for cost and performance estimates, and apply linear interpolation/normalization for turbines under 2,000 MMBtu/h when estimating achievable efficiencies and emissions rates. Recognize that smaller units will typically have higher CCS costs per MWh.

rubrics_metrics.name: F-factor definition for emissions calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: An F factor is the ratio of the gas volume of the products of combustion to the heat content of the fuel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the F-factor in heat-input and mass-balance-based emissions calculations where required; ensure the appropriate F-factor for the specific fuel and combustion process is applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to ISO/CSA/ANSI ISO 27916:2019 for CO2 storage using EOR
rubrics_metrics.description: International Standards Organization (ISO) standard designated as CSA Group (CSA)/American National Standards Institute (ANSI) ISO 27916:2019, Carbon Dioxide Capture, Transportation and Geological Storage—Carbon Dioxide Storage Using Enhanced Oil Recovery (referred to as 'CSA/ANSI ISO 27916:2019').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating CO2 storage and EOR-related reporting/monitoring approaches, consult and align with CSA/ANSI ISO 27916:2019 where applicable, particularly for storage quantification and monitoring practices referenced by EPA subparts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of cost reductions from learning-by-doing and technological development
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA expects costs to decrease due to learning by doing and technological development; examples include sustained deployment experiences that reduced capital costs in other power-generation projects (e.g., nuclear reactors in South Korea yielding a 13 percent reduction in capital costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include projected cost declines from deployment-driven learning and innovation when conducting long-term cost forecasting or scenario analysis. Document assumptions about the pace and magnitude of learning effects and justify parallels to historical deployment examples when used.
